title: Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
hook: the king sees, takes, and arranges a loyal husband's death

segments.voice: Yesterday Jonathan's son got a seat at David's table, kept for him always. Your line was always at my table. Today, the same king, in a chapter that turns against him.

At the turn of the year, the text says, the time when kings go out to battle, David sends his general Joab, his servants and the whole army. And David stays in Jerusalem. That one detail sits at the start of the chapter like a stone in a shoe: the king isn't where kings go. One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the roof of the king's house. From the roof he sees a woman washing herself, and she is very beautiful. He doesn't look away. He sends someone to find out who she is.
screen: `WHEN KINGS GO OUT TO BATTLE.` → `DAVID STAYS IN JERUSALEM.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: The answer comes back: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite, who is away fighting in David's own army. Listen to the verbs, all of them the king's. He sees. He sends. He takes. The text gives Bathsheba almost no words; the few she sends are a message: I am with child. Then David starts covering. He calls Uriah home from the front: go down to your house. Uriah sleeps at the palace door with the servants instead. The ark and Israel and Judah are in tents, he says, and Joab is camped in the open field; how could I go home, eat and drink, and lie with my wife? David gets him drunk. He still won't go home. So David writes Joab a letter and sends it with Uriah himself: put him at the front of the hardest fighting, then pull back, so he's struck down. Uriah carries his own death in his hand. It happens. David's reply to Joab sounds almost calm: don't let this thing be evil in your eyes; the sword devours one as well as another. Bathsheba mourns her husband, and then David brings her into his house. And the narrator, silent about right and wrong all chapter, speaks once: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." In Hebrew it's an echo. Let it not be evil in your eyes, says David. It was evil in the eyes of the Lord, says the narrator. The king could see a woman on a roof. He couldn't see what he was doing.
screen: `HE SEES. HE SENDS. HE TAKES.` · `URIAH WON'T GO HOME.` · `THE LETTER IN URIAH'S HAND.` · then, large: `IT DISPLEASED THE LORD.` · then: `HE COULDN'T SEE HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Power turns up in ordinary places: over a child, an employee, a waiter, someone who owes you. Let one of those places come to mind and ask, quietly, what your power lets you not notice about this person, because you don't have to. Don't punish yourself; just name one thing, and if you pray, you can hold it before God.
Bathsheba. The woman the king saw, sent for and took, while her loyal husband slept at the palace door. Today's word.
Your line: power can blind. The narrator sees what the king won't see. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of David and Bathsheba in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the next chapter, the prophet Nathan's rebuke, is read as part of the same story.

chat.says: Isn't the David and Bathsheba story basically a romance?
options: No: the king sees, sends and takes, then arranges her husband's death.

chat.meaning: The chapter's verbs are David's: he sees, sends, takes, then has Uriah killed; the narrator says it displeased the Lord.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of 2 Samuel 11:27 (certain in the KJV).
The Hebrew echo between 11:25 (al yera b'eineikha) and 11:27 (vayera ... b'einei) is stated; please confirm.
'At the turn of the year' paraphrases 11:1 ('the return of the year').
Bathsheba is presented without blame; the text gives her few words (11:5). Rabbinic readings that soften David's guilt (e.g. Shabbat 56a) are left out; a Keeper may want to add one.
Nathan's parable is left for the next day.
Editor: cut the invented 'he can see a lot of the city' (11:2 says only 'from the roof'), and softened the sweeping 'everyone has power somewhere' in the practice.
